title: The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)
dateDisplay: canon took shape c. 400 BC – AD 100
summary: The Jewish Scriptures in three parts — Law, Prophets, Writings — which became the Christian Old Testament.
article:
The Jewish Scriptures are the *Tanakh*, an acronym for their three sections: **Torah** (Law, the five books of Moses), **Nevi'im** (Prophets, from Joshua through Malachi), and **Ketuvim** (Writings — Psalms, wisdom, and the rest). Christians received these same books as the **Old Testament**, though they reorder them and, in most traditions, count them differently.

*What the texts claim:* the Torah presents itself as the covenant law given through Moses, the Prophets as the word of the LORD to Israel, the Writings as Israel's prayer, wisdom, and memory.

*What history can trace:* the canon closed in stages, not by a single decree. The Torah was authoritative by the time of Ezra (5th c. BC); the Prophets by roughly the 2nd c. BC (the prologue to the book of Sirach, c. 132 BC, already speaks of "the Law, the Prophets, and the other books"); the Writings remained somewhat fluid into the 1st c. AD. The old idea of a formal "Council of Jamnia" fixing the canon around AD 90 is now generally regarded as a scholarly myth — the boundaries settled gradually through use.

The number of books differs by tradition: Jews and Protestants count the same 39 (24 in the Hebrew reckoning); Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include the deuterocanonical books that came through the Greek Septuagint. That fault line is taken up in the New Testament canon batch.
readingPointer: Jesus names the three-part shape in Luke 24:44 — "the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms."

traditions.protestant: 39 books, matching the Hebrew Tanakh (reckoned as 24 in Jewish tradition).
traditions.catholic: 46 books, adding the deuterocanon (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees, plus additions to Esther and Daniel) via the Septuagint.
traditions.orthodox: A slightly larger canon still, including books such as 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, and Psalm 151.

title: Genesis
dateDisplay: final form c. 6th–5th c. BC · traditionally Moses (c. 15th–13th c. BC)
summary: The book of beginnings — creation, the fall, the flood, and the patriarchs from Abraham to Joseph.
article:
*Genesis* ("beginning") runs from creation to the death of Joseph in Egypt: the making of the world, the first humans and the fall, Cain and Abel, the flood, Babel, and then the family chosen through Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph.

*Traditional register:* Jewish and Christian tradition ascribes the Torah — Genesis included — to **Moses**, writing in roughly the 15th–13th century BC.

*Historical register:* since the 18th–19th centuries most critical scholars have read the Torah as woven from several strands (the **Documentary Hypothesis** — the Yahwistic, Elohistic, Deuteronomic, and Priestly sources), combined and edited into their present form during and after the Babylonian exile, roughly the 6th–5th c. BC. The theory has been much revised and is not universally held, but the great majority of scholars agree the Torah reached its final shape long after Moses. This node sits at that estimated final form; the dotted tether runs back to the events Genesis narrates.

The two registers need not be collapsed: one can hold that the book carries Mosaic tradition faithfully while acknowledging that its written composition was a longer process. The dating is genuinely contested, and this entry marks the disagreement rather than settling it.

title: Exodus
dateDisplay: final form c. 6th–5th c. BC · traditionally Moses
summary: Israel's deliverance from Egypt, the crossing of the sea, and the covenant at Sinai.
article:
*Exodus* tells of Israel's slavery in Egypt, the call of Moses, the plagues and the Passover, the crossing of the sea, and the covenant given at Sinai — including the Ten Commandments and the pattern for the tabernacle. It is the Old Testament's central story of redemption.

*Traditional register:* attributed to Moses, as the second of the five books of the Torah.

*Historical register:* like the rest of the Torah, critical scholarship sees Exodus as combining older narrative traditions with a substantial Priestly contribution (especially the tabernacle chapters), reaching final form in the exilic or post-exilic period. The date of the events it describes is itself disputed (a 15th- or a 13th-century exodus — see the earlier entry), which is a separate question from when the book was written.

The book's own claim, its traditional authorship, and its critical composition history are three distinct registers; this entry keeps them apart rather than flattening one into another.

title: Leviticus
dateDisplay: final form c. 6th–5th c. BC · traditionally Moses
summary: The priestly handbook of sacrifice, purity, and holiness given at Sinai.
article:
*Leviticus* is the ritual and moral core of the Torah: laws of sacrifice, the ordination of priests, clean and unclean, the Day of Atonement, and the "Holiness Code" (chs. 17–26) with its refrain, "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy."

*Traditional register:* Mosaic, delivered at Sinai.

*Historical register:* critical scholarship assigns Leviticus almost entirely to the **Priestly** source, the latest major strand of the Torah, generally dated to the exilic or early post-exilic period — which is why this node sits near the end of the Torah cluster. Some scholars argue the Holiness Code preserves older material later edited into the Priestly framework.

The book's picture of worship deeply shaped both Judaism and the New Testament's language of sacrifice and atonement, whatever the date of its final composition.

title: Numbers
dateDisplay: final form c. 6th–5th c. BC · traditionally Moses
summary: Israel's forty years in the wilderness, from Sinai to the edge of the promised land.
article:
*Numbers* (named for its two censuses) follows Israel from Sinai through the wilderness to the plains of Moab: the rebellions, the spies, the bronze serpent, Balaam's oracles, and the slow dying-out of the exodus generation.

*Traditional register:* Mosaic.

*Historical register:* critical analysis finds both older narrative material and heavy Priestly editing, with final composition in the exilic/post-exilic period, consistent with the rest of the Torah. This node sits at that estimated final form; its tether runs back to the wilderness wanderings it recounts.

As with the other books of the Torah, the traditional attribution to Moses and the critical account of a longer editorial process are held here side by side, with the dating openly marked as disputed.

title: Deuteronomy
dateDisplay: Deuteronomic core c. 622 BC (Josiah's reform) · traditionally Moses
summary: Moses' final speeches to Israel — the covenant restated on the edge of the promised land.
article:
*Deuteronomy* ("second law") is cast as Moses' farewell addresses on the plains of Moab, restating the covenant for the generation about to enter Canaan. It contains the *Shema* ("Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one"), the great commandment to love God, and covenant blessings and curses.

*Traditional register:* the last book of the Torah, spoken by Moses (whose death it records in the closing chapter — a detail that troubled even ancient readers).

*Historical register:* Deuteronomy is the best-anchored book of the Torah for critical dating. Since W. M. L. de Wette (1805), many scholars have identified its core with the "Book of the Law" found in the temple during King **Josiah's reform in 622 BC** (2 Kings 22), which triggered a centralization of worship matching Deuteronomy's demands. On this view the book (or its core) was composed or promulgated in the late 7th century, then expanded in the exile. This is why this node sits earlier than the other four — a deliberate, honest reflection of where the evidence points.

Deuteronomy's theology went on to shape the whole "Deuteronomistic History" (Joshua–Kings).
readingPointer: Read it: Deuteronomy 6, then 2 Kings 22 for the scroll found under Josiah.

title: Joshua, Judges, Samuel & Kings
summary: The narrative of Israel from the conquest to the exile — the Hebrew canon's "Former Prophets."
article:
In the Hebrew canon these four books (Samuel and Kings each counted as one) are the **Former Prophets**: the story of Israel in the land, from Joshua's conquest, through the chaotic era of the judges, the rise of the monarchy under Saul and David, the temple of Solomon, the divided kingdom, and finally the fall of Samaria (722 BC) and Jerusalem (586 BC).

*Traditional register:* Jewish tradition variously ascribed these to Joshua, Samuel, and Jeremiah.

*Historical register:* since Martin Noth (1943), most scholars read them as a single, theologically unified **Deuteronomistic History**, written from the standpoint of Deuteronomy — judging each king by his faithfulness to centralized worship. A first edition is often dated to Josiah's reign (late 7th c.), updated after the exile began, which is where this node sits. The books draw on older sources (court records, prophetic legends, the "Book of Jashar").

Ruth, which the Christian order places after Judges, belongs in the Hebrew canon not here but among the Writings — one of several small differences in how the traditions arrange the same books.
readingPointer: The individual figures and events — Joshua, David, Solomon, the exile — each have their own nodes; the dotted tether links this scroll to the conquest where its story opens.

title: Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah & Esther
summary: The post-exilic retelling of Israel's story and the restoration under Persia.
article:
These later histories look back on Israel from after the exile. **Chronicles** retells the story from Adam's genealogy to the return, centring on David, the temple, and worship. **Ezra** and **Nehemiah** recount the return from Babylon, the rebuilding of the temple and Jerusalem's walls, and the renewal of the covenant under Persian rule. **Esther**, set in the Persian court, tells how a Jewish queen saved her people — and, famously, never once names God.

*Historical register:* Chronicles–Ezra–Nehemiah are usually dated to the 5th–4th century BC (the "Chronicler"), drawing on and reshaping the earlier books of Samuel and Kings. Esther's date and historicity are debated; many place its composition in the later Persian or Hellenistic period.

The events themselves — the fall of Jerusalem, the exile, the return under Cyrus — have their own nodes and strong external attestation; this entry concerns the books that record them.
readingPointer: Read it: Ezra 1 and Nehemiah 1–6 for the return; Esther for the Persian court.

traditions.protestant: Esther is the short Hebrew (Masoretic) text.
traditions.catholic: Includes the longer Greek Esther, with additions (prayers, the king's decrees) that name God explicitly.
traditions.orthodox: Also receives the longer Greek Esther and, in some canons, 1 Esdras.

title: Psalms
dateDisplay: individual psalms 10th–3rd c. BC · Psalter compiled by c. 3rd c. BC
summary: Israel's book of prayer and praise — 150 psalms gathered over centuries.
article:
The **Psalter** is Israel's hymnbook and prayer book: 150 poems of praise, lament, thanksgiving, trust, and kingship, arranged in five "books." It is the most quoted Old Testament book in the New Testament.

*Traditional register:* 73 psalms carry the heading "of David," and tradition names David — the musician-king — as the psalmist, giving the book its royal association. The tether on this node runs back to David for that reason.

*Historical register:* the psalm headings are ancient but not necessarily authorial (the Hebrew *le-David* can mean "for" or "belonging to" David as much as "by" him). Scholars see psalms composed across many centuries — some perhaps from the monarchy, many from the exile and after — gradually collected into the fivefold Psalter by roughly the 3rd century BC, where this node sits. A few psalms (e.g. Ps. 137, "by the waters of Babylon") are plainly exilic.

So the book is at once traditionally Davidic and, as a *collection*, the work of centuries — both true, on different registers.

title: Proverbs
dateDisplay: collections 10th–5th c. BC · compiled by c. 5th–4th c. BC
summary: Israel's collected wisdom — practical sayings on the fear of the LORD and the ordered life.
article:
*Proverbs* gathers Israel's wisdom tradition: short sayings and longer poems on prudence, speech, work, justice, and the "fear of the LORD" as the beginning of wisdom. Wisdom herself is personified, crying out in the streets and present with God at creation.

*Traditional register:* headed "the proverbs of **Solomon**" (1:1), the wise king, and traditionally ascribed to him — hence the tether back to Solomon.

*Historical register:* the book itself names several collections and other authors ("the men of Hezekiah," "the words of Agur," "the words of King Lemuel"), so it is plainly an anthology assembled over time and finalized in the post-exilic period. Its earliest core may well reflect the Solomonic court's patronage of wisdom; parts show striking parallels to the older Egyptian *Instruction of Amenemope*.

The Solomonic attribution and the layered composition are both real; the node sits at the estimated final compilation.
readingPointer: Read it: Proverbs 1–9, then the sayings that follow.

title: Job
dateDisplay: date uncertain, likely 6th–4th c. BC · setting is patriarchal
summary: The great poem on innocent suffering — Job's ordeal and God's answer from the whirlwind.
article:
*Job* is the Bible's most searching treatment of undeserved suffering: a blameless man loses everything, argues with friends who insist he must have sinned, and finally hears God answer not with explanation but out of a whirlwind, with the wonders of creation.

*Setting vs. composition:* the story is set in the patriarchal age (Job lives like a patriarch, with no reference to Israel, the law, or the temple) — which is why the older "Job the man" node sits far to the left. But the *book*, a sophisticated poetic drama framed by a prose folktale, is generally dated much later, most often to the 6th–4th century BC. This node marks the book; its tether runs back to the patriarchal setting.

*Historical register:* authorship is unknown, and the dating is genuinely uncertain — estimates range widely. What is not in doubt is the book's stature as one of the summits of world literature and of Israel's wisdom.
readingPointer: Read it: Job 1–2, then the whirlwind speeches of Job 38–42.

title: Ecclesiastes
dateDisplay: c. 3rd c. BC (late Hebrew) · traditionally Solomon
summary: The Preacher's meditation on the fleeting nature of life — "vanity of vanities."
article:
*Ecclesiastes* is the words of **Qoheleth**, "the Preacher," who tests pleasure, wealth, work, and wisdom and finds them all *hevel* — vapour, fleeting breath, "vanity." Yet the book ends by commending the simple gifts of God and the fear of God.

*Traditional register:* the Preacher calls himself "son of David, king in Jerusalem" (1:1), and tradition read this as **Solomon** in his old age — hence the tether to Solomon.

*Historical register:* the book's Hebrew is late, showing Aramaic and possibly Persian influence, and its questioning tone fits the Hellenistic age; most scholars date it to about the 3rd century BC, long after Solomon, with the Solomonic frame a literary device. Its place in the canon was debated in antiquity precisely because of its bracing skepticism.

The traditional Solomonic voice and the late linguistic evidence are the two registers held together here.
readingPointer: Read it: Ecclesiastes 1–3 and the close of chapter 12.

title: Song of Songs
dateDisplay: date debated, c. 5th–3rd c. BC · traditionally Solomon
summary: A cycle of love poems, read as human love and as the love between God and his people.
article:
The *Song of Songs* (Song of Solomon) is a lyrical cycle of love poetry between a bride and her beloved — sensuous, tender, and unabashed. It never mentions God directly.

*Traditional register:* titled "the Song of Songs, which is Solomon's," and traditionally ascribed to Solomon; the tether runs back to him. Both Jewish and Christian tradition also read it allegorically — as the love between the LORD and Israel, or between Christ and the Church — which is largely why it was received into the canon.

*Historical register:* its language and imagery suggest a later date to most scholars, often the Persian or Hellenistic period (5th–3rd c. BC), though some argue for older material; authorship is unknown and the Solomonic title likely honorific.

Whether read as human love celebrated or divine love figured, the book's place in Scripture rested on that double reading.
readingPointer: Read it: Song of Songs 2 and 8.

title: Isaiah
dateDisplay: chs. 1–39 c. 8th c. BC · chs. 40–66 c. 6th c. BC (composite)
summary: The greatest of the prophetic books — judgment, comfort, and the Servant who suffers.
article:
*Isaiah* is the most far-reaching of the prophetic books, moving from 8th-century warnings to Judah, through the promise of comfort to the exiles, to a vision of new heavens and a new earth. It gives Christianity some of its most cherished texts — Immanuel, the child born to us, and the Suffering Servant of chapter 53.

*Traditional register:* ascribed whole to **Isaiah of Jerusalem**, who prophesied c. 740–700 BC; the tether runs back to that prophet.

*Historical register:* since the late 18th century most scholars have divided the book. **First Isaiah** (chs. 1–39) reflects the 8th-century Assyrian crisis; **Second Isaiah** (40–55) plainly addresses exiles in Babylon and even names Cyrus of Persia (d. 530 BC), pointing to a 6th-century hand; **Third Isaiah** (56–66) fits the early post-exilic community. On this reading the book is a composite growing across two centuries around Isaiah's legacy — this node sits in the exilic middle. Traditional interpreters counter that a prophet could foresee Cyrus by name.

It is the classic case of the wider debate over prophetic books, and this entry lays out the disagreement plainly.
readingPointer: Read it: Isaiah 6 (the call), 40 (comfort), and 53 (the Servant).

title: Jeremiah & Lamentations
dateDisplay: compiled c. 6th c. BC · Hebrew (MT) and Greek (LXX) editions differ
summary: The weeping prophet's oracles through Jerusalem's fall — and the laments over the ruined city.
article:
*Jeremiah* records the ministry of the prophet through the last decades of Judah, the Babylonian siege, and the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC — a searing mix of oracles, laments, and narrative, including the promise of a **new covenant** written on the heart (31:31–34). *Lamentations*, five acrostic poems mourning the destroyed city, is traditionally paired with him.

*Traditional register:* the oracles are Jeremiah's, dictated (the book says) to his scribe **Baruch**; Lamentations is traditionally ascribed to Jeremiah as well.

*Historical register:* the book grew in stages — Baruch's scroll, expanded with prose sermons and narrative. Strikingly, the **Greek Septuagint text of Jeremiah is about one-eighth shorter** than the Hebrew Masoretic text and orders the material differently; fragments of both editions appear at Qumran, showing the book still circulated in more than one form. Lamentations stands in the Hebrew canon among the Writings, not with Jeremiah, and its authorship is uncertain.

The node sits near the exile; its tether runs back to the prophet.
readingPointer: Read it: Jeremiah 1 and 31, then Lamentations 3.

traditions.catholic: Adds Baruch (with the Letter of Jeremiah) among the deuterocanonical books.
traditions.orthodox: Likewise receives Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah.

title: Ezekiel
summary: Visions of God's glory in exile — the wheels, the dry bones, and the new temple.
article:
*Ezekiel*, a priest deported to Babylon, prophesies among the exiles in astonishing visions: the throne-chariot with its wheels within wheels, the glory departing the temple, the valley of dry bones brought to life, and a vast blueprint for a restored temple. It moves from judgment to the promise of a new heart and a new spirit.

*Historical register:* the book is closely tied to its dated setting — its oracles carry precise dates across the exile (593–571 BC), and scholarship generally accepts a strong core from the prophet himself, edited by his circle. That gives it a firmer footing than Isaiah's authorship debate, though the extent of later editing is discussed.

The node sits within the exilic period it so vividly inhabits, tethered to the prophet Ezekiel.
readingPointer: Read it: Ezekiel 1 (the vision), 37 (the dry bones).

title: Daniel
dateDisplay: final form c. 165 BC (Maccabean crisis) · set in the 6th c. BC · traditionally 6th c.
summary: Court tales and apocalyptic visions of the kingdoms of the world and the kingdom of God.
article:
*Daniel* falls in two halves: **court tales** of faithful Jews in the Babylonian and Persian courts (the fiery furnace, the writing on the wall, the lions' den) and **apocalyptic visions** of successive world empires giving way at last to "one like a son of man" and the kingdom of God.

*This is the timeline's sharpest setting-vs-composition gap.* The book is *set* in the 6th-century Babylonian exile, and tradition dates it there — which is why the older "Daniel" figure node sits at c. 605 BC. But the long dotted tether reaches all the way from there to **c. 165 BC**, where this node sits, because most critical scholars date the book's final form to the crisis under **Antiochus IV Epiphanes** and the Maccabean revolt: the visions track Greek history in detail down to Antiochus, then become inexact about his death — the usual marker of writing *during* those events. The court tales may rework older material. In the Hebrew canon, tellingly, Daniel is placed not among the Prophets but among the Writings.

Traditional interpreters read the precise "prophecy" as genuine foresight. The two positions are laid out here; the placement follows the critical dating Jamie chose for book nodes, and the tether makes the gap visible rather than hiding it.
readingPointer: Read it: Daniel 3 and 6 (the tales), then 7 (the vision).

traditions.catholic: Adds the Greek portions — the Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three, Susanna, and Bel and the Dragon.
traditions.orthodox: Likewise receives the Greek additions to Daniel.

title: The Twelve (Minor Prophets)
dateDisplay: prophets 8th–5th c. BC · collected as one scroll by c. 3rd c. BC
summary: The twelve shorter prophetic books, copied together on a single scroll.
article:
The **Book of the Twelve** gathers the shorter prophetic books — Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi — which fit together on one scroll and were counted in antiquity as a single book. "Minor" refers only to their length, not their weight.

*Historical register:* the twelve span roughly three centuries — Amos and Hosea in the 8th-century north, others through the Assyrian and Babylonian crises, and Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi in the post-exilic restoration. They were compiled into a deliberately ordered collection by about the 3rd century BC, where this node sits; the tether runs back to the grouped "Minor Prophets" figure of the prophetic age.

Several of them raise their own questions — Jonah's genre (history or parable) and Joel's date are debated — which are noted with the prophets themselves rather than repeated here.
readingPointer: Read a few: Amos 5, Micah 6, Jonah, and Malachi.
